blocks.text: Educational Management: Educational management organises people, resources and activities to achieve educational objectives. Functions: Major functions include planning, organising, directing, coordinating, supervising and controlling. Leadership: Educational leadership guides and motivates members of an institution toward common educational goals. Decision Making: Decision making involves selecting suitable courses of action after considering alternatives and available information.
Meaning: Educational management is the coordination of human, material and financial resources through planning, organising, directing and controlling to achieve educational objectives effectively.
Functions: Gulick's POSDCORB (planning, organising, staffing, directing, coordinating, reporting and budgeting), along with supervision and evaluation, describe the main managerial functions.

Leadership: Educational leaders may be autocratic, democratic or laissez-faire; transformational and instructional leadership are particularly effective for improving schools. Good leaders inspire, communicate, motivate and build teamwork.

Decision making: A systematic decision-making process - defining the problem, collecting data, generating and evaluating alternatives, choosing, implementing and reviewing - leads to better outcomes. Participative decision-making increases commitment of staff and stakeholders.

sections.title: Unit IV – Management of Educational Institutions

blocks.text: Institutional Management: It includes management of staff, students, timetable, records, finance, infrastructure and academic work. Head of Institution: The head provides leadership, coordination, supervision and administrative direction. Supervision: Educational supervision helps improve teaching, staff performance and institutional functioning. Quality Management: Quality management requires clear goals, monitoring, cooperation, evaluation and continuous improvement.
Institutional management: Managing academics, staff, students, records, finance and physical resources ensures smooth functioning of schools and colleges.
Head of institution: The head is the leader, administrator, supervisor and coordinator responsible for planning, discipline, academic quality, finances and community relations.
Supervision: Modern supervision is democratic and supportive, using classroom observation, workshops, demonstration lessons and feedback to improve teaching.

Quality management: TQM, IQACs, accreditation, school self-evaluation and stakeholder feedback promote continuous improvement. Effective institutional management creates a positive climate where teachers teach well and students learn well.

sections.title: EDU 305 – MENTAL HEALTH AND HYGIENE
SHORT NOTES
Unit I – Mental Health and Hygiene

blocks.text: Mental Health. A balanced state that enables a person to think, feel, work and adjust effectively.
Mental Hygiene. Principles and practices for preserving mental health and preventing emotional and behavioural difficulties.
Objectives. Mental hygiene promotes adjustment, emotional balance, healthy personality and prevention of mental problems.
Determinants. Family environment, child rearing, social conditions and psychological factors influence mental health.

Mental health in detail. The WHO describes mental health as a state of well-being in which a person realises their abilities, copes with normal stresses, works productively and contributes to the community. It is not merely the absence of mental illness; it includes emotional balance, realistic self-concept and good social relations.

Mental hygiene in detail. The mental hygiene movement was started by Clifford Beers ('A Mind That Found Itself', 1908). Mental hygiene includes preventive measures (healthy environment, guidance), preservative measures (maintaining good mental health) and curative measures (early treatment).

Objectives in detail. Preservation of mental health, prevention of mental disorders, early identification and treatment, development of integrated personality, healthy adjustment in home, school and society, and public awareness to reduce stigma.

Determinants in detail. Biological factors (heredity, health, nervous system), family factors (child rearing, parental relations, broken homes), school factors (teacher behaviour, curriculum load, examinations), social factors (poverty, discrimination, peer pressure, media) and psychological factors (stress, frustration, conflict, self-esteem).

sections.title: Unit II – Personality and Mental Health

blocks.text: Wholesome Personality. Shows balanced development, realistic self-understanding, emotional stability and healthy relationships.
Abnormal Personality. Refers to seriously maladaptive patterns that interfere with healthy functioning.
Mentally Healthy Person. Shows self-acceptance, realistic thinking, emotional control, good relationships and capacity for adjustment.
Classification. Classification of abnormal behaviour helps organise and understand different patterns of disturbance.

Wholesome personality in detail. It is an integrated personality with realistic self-understanding, emotional maturity, social adjustment, sense of responsibility, a clear philosophy of life and consistent behaviour. It develops through supportive home and school environments.

Abnormal personality in detail. Abnormality is judged by deviation from statistical norms, violation of social norms, personal distress and maladaptive behaviour. Causes can be biological, psychological and social. Examples include anxiety, depression, phobias and personality disorders.

Mentally healthy person in detail. According to Marie Jahoda, criteria include positive attitude toward self, growth and self-actualisation, integration, autonomy, accurate perception of reality and environmental mastery. Such a person copes with stress, maintains satisfying relationships and works productively.

Classification in detail. Traditionally, disorders are classified into neuroses (anxiety, phobia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, hysteria) and psychoses (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder). Modern systems are DSM-5 and ICD-11, which include categories like anxiety disorders, mood disorders, neurodevelopmental disorders, personality disorders and substance use disorders.

sections.title: Unit III – Diagnostic and Remedial Techniques

blocks.text: Play Therapy. Uses play as a means of expression and therapeutic help, especially for children.
Behaviour Therapy. Uses learning principles to modify maladaptive behaviour and strengthen adaptive behaviour.
Counselling Therapy. Uses a supportive helping relationship to understand problems and improve adjustment.
Remedial Purpose. These methods seek better emotional, behavioural and social functioning.

Play therapy in detail. Developed by Anna Freud, Melanie Klein and Virginia Axline, play therapy allows children to express feelings and conflicts through toys, dolls, sand, clay, puppets and drawing. The therapist observes and helps the child understand and resolve emotions. It is useful for trauma, anxiety and behaviour problems.

Behaviour therapy in detail. Based on Pavlov, Watson and Skinner, it treats maladaptive behaviour as learned and modifiable. Techniques include positive reinforcement, token economy, systematic desensitisation (Wolpe), modelling (Bandura), aversion therapy and shaping.

Counselling therapy in detail. Includes client-centred therapy (Rogers), cognitive-behavioural therapy (Beck), rational emotive behaviour therapy (Ellis) and group counselling. It helps individuals gain insight, change negative thinking and develop coping skills.

Remedial purpose in detail. These techniques aim to reduce emotional distress, correct maladaptive behaviour, improve adjustment and social skills, and restore healthy functioning. Teachers can use simple behavioural techniques and refer students to professionals when necessary.

sections.title: Unit IV – Adjustment and Mental Conflict

blocks.text: Adjustment. The process of balancing personal needs with environmental demands.
Maladjustment. Persistent difficulty in responding effectively to personal or environmental demands.
Adjustment Mechanisms. Ways individuals cope with frustration, stress and conflict.
Mental Conflict. Occurs when motives, goals or choices are incompatible; guidance, counselling and realistic coping can help resolve it.

Adjustment in detail. Adjustment is a continuous process by which a person changes behaviour to achieve harmony between personal needs and environmental demands. Areas include home, school, health, social and emotional adjustment.

Maladjustment in detail. Signs include aggression, withdrawal, anxiety, truancy, lying, stealing, poor academic performance and nervous habits. Causes include unhealthy home conditions, school pressure, physical problems, social factors and repeated frustration.

Adjustment mechanisms in detail. Defence mechanisms described by Freud include repression, rationalisation, projection, displacement, regression, sublimation, compensation, identification and day-dreaming. Moderate use reduces anxiety, but excessive use avoids reality. Direct coping such as problem-solving is healthier.

Mental conflict in detail. Lewin's types: approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance, approach-avoidance and double approach-avoidance. Conflicts cause tension and indecision; remedies include clear values, realistic goals, careful decision-making, guidance and counselling, and stress management.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
Unit I – Mental Health and Hygiene

blocks.text: Mental Health: A balanced state that enables a person to think, feel, work and adjust effectively. Mental Hygiene: Principles and practices for preserving mental health and preventing emotional and behavioural difficulties. Objectives: Mental hygiene promotes adjustment, emotional balance, healthy personality and prevention of mental problems. Determinants: Family environment, child rearing, social conditions and psychological factors influence mental health.
Mental health: Mental health is a state of well-being involving emotional balance, realistic thinking, productive work and good relationships, not just the absence of illness.
Mental hygiene: It is the science and practice of preserving mental health, preventing disorders and treating them early. Its pioneer was Clifford Beers.
Objectives: To preserve mental health, prevent mental illness, cure disorders early, develop an integrated personality and promote healthy adjustment.

Determinants: Heredity and health, family environment and child rearing, school climate, peer group, socio-economic conditions and psychological factors like stress and self-esteem determine mental health. Schools can promote mental hygiene through a friendly climate, guidance services, life-skills education and early identification of problems.

sections.title: Unit II – Personality and Mental Health

blocks.text: Wholesome Personality: Shows balanced development, realistic self-understanding, emotional stability and healthy relationships. Abnormal Personality: Refers to seriously maladaptive patterns that interfere with healthy functioning. Mentally Healthy Person: Shows self-acceptance, realistic thinking, emotional control, good relationships and capacity for adjustment. Classification: Classification of abnormal behaviour helps organise and understand different patterns of disturbance.
Wholesome personality: An integrated personality shows self-understanding, emotional maturity, social adjustment and responsibility.
Abnormal personality: Persistent maladaptive patterns that cause distress and interfere with functioning, arising from biological, psychological and social causes.
Mentally healthy person: Jahoda's criteria - positive self-attitude, growth, integration, autonomy, accurate perception of reality and environmental mastery - describe mental health.

Classification: Neuroses and psychoses in traditional terms, and DSM-5 and ICD-11 categories in modern terms, help professionals diagnose and treat disorders. Teachers should know basic signs to identify students who need help.

sections.title: Unit III – Diagnostic and Remedial Techniques

blocks.text: Play Therapy: Uses play as a means of expression and therapeutic help, especially for children. Behaviour Therapy: Uses learning principles to modify maladaptive behaviour and strengthen adaptive behaviour. Counselling Therapy: Uses a supportive helping relationship to understand problems and improve adjustment. Remedial Purpose: These methods seek better emotional, behavioural and social functioning.
Play therapy: It uses play materials to help children express and work through emotions they cannot verbalise, and is effective for young children with anxiety or trauma.
Behaviour therapy: It applies learning principles - reinforcement, desensitisation, token economy, modelling - to replace maladaptive behaviour with adaptive behaviour.
Counselling therapy: Client-centred, cognitive-behavioural and group counselling provide a supportive relationship to help individuals understand problems and develop coping strategies.

Remedial purpose and role of teachers: These techniques aim at better emotional, behavioural and social functioning. Teachers can contribute through observation, simple behaviour modification, supportive relationships and referral to counsellors and psychologists.

sections.title: Unit IV – Adjustment and Mental Conflict

blocks.text: Adjustment: The process of balancing personal needs with environmental demands. Maladjustment: Persistent difficulty in responding effectively to personal or environmental demands. Adjustment Mechanisms: Ways individuals cope with frustration, stress and conflict. Mental Conflict: Occurs when motives, goals or choices are incompatible; guidance, counselling and realistic coping can help resolve it.
Adjustment: Adjustment means achieving harmony between one's needs and the demands of the environment, shown by emotional balance, social acceptance and realistic goals.
Maladjustment: Persistent difficulty in coping, shown through aggression, withdrawal, anxiety and poor performance, caused by home, school, personal and social factors.

Adjustment mechanisms: Defence mechanisms like repression, rationalisation, projection, displacement, regression, sublimation and compensation reduce anxiety but should not replace realistic problem-solving.

Mental conflict: Approach-approach, avoidance-avoidance and approach-avoidance conflicts cause tension. Guidance, counselling, clear values, realistic decision-making and stress management help resolve conflicts and promote healthy adjustment.

sections.title: EDU 306 – LIFE SKILLS EDUCATION
SHORT NOTES
Unit I – Life Skills

blocks.text: Life Skills. Abilities that help individuals deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life.
Need and Importance. Life skills support healthy decisions, relationships, adjustment, confidence and responsible behaviour.
Life Skills Education. An educational process for developing practical psychosocial abilities through participation and experience.
Role of Education. Schools and teachers can deliberately develop life skills through activities, discussion, practice and reflection.

Life skills in detail. WHO (1997) defines life skills as abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that enable individuals to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life. WHO identified ten core life skills: self-awareness, empathy, critical thinking, creative thinking, decision making, problem solving, effective communication, interpersonal relationships, coping with stress and coping with emotions.

Need and importance in detail. Young people face peer pressure, substance abuse, academic stress, relationship problems, career choices and digital risks. Life skills help them make healthy choices, prevent risky behaviour, improve mental health, build confidence and become responsible citizens.

Life skills education in detail. It is a participatory, experiential approach using role plays, group discussions, case studies, games, brainstorming, debates and storytelling. In India it is integrated into the Adolescence Education Programme, School Health Programme under Ayushman Bharat and NEP 2020.

Role of education in detail. Schools can provide a safe environment, train teachers as facilitators, integrate life skills into subjects and co-curricular activities, involve parents and community, and use counselling services. Teachers should model these skills themselves.

sections.title: Unit II – Thinking and Decision Skills

blocks.text: Critical Thinking. The ability to examine information and ideas carefully before accepting conclusions.
Creative Thinking. The ability to generate new, useful and flexible ideas.
Decision Making. The ability to choose among alternatives after considering possible consequences.
Problem Solving. The ability to identify a problem, examine causes and alternatives and select a workable solution.

Critical thinking in detail. It involves analysing information, questioning assumptions, evaluating evidence, recognising bias and drawing logical conclusions. It helps students resist misinformation, peer pressure and advertising, and make informed choices. Teachers develop it through open-ended questions, debates, case studies and analysis of media.

Creative thinking in detail. It involves fluency, flexibility, originality and elaboration (Guilford, Torrance). It helps find new solutions, adapt to change and express oneself. Activities like brainstorming, art, storytelling, projects and 'what if' questions develop it.

Decision making in detail. Steps: identify the decision, gather information, list alternatives, consider consequences (pros and cons), choose the best option, act and evaluate. Good decision-making helps in matters such as career choice, health, relationships and avoiding risky behaviour.

Problem solving in detail. Steps: identify and define the problem, find its causes, generate possible solutions, evaluate them, select and implement a solution, and review results. It reduces stress and helps individuals deal with challenges constructively.

sections.title: Unit III – Social and Communication Skills

blocks.text: Effective Communication. Clear and appropriate expression together with careful listening and understanding.
Interpersonal Relationship. The ability to establish and maintain healthy relationships with others.
Empathy. The ability to understand another person's feelings and point of view.
Cooperation. Working constructively with others toward shared goals.

Effective communication in detail. It includes verbal and non-verbal expression, active listening, assertiveness (expressing one's views respectfully), giving and receiving feedback and saying 'no' to undesirable pressure. Barriers include poor listening, emotions and prejudice. Role plays and group discussions develop it.

Interpersonal relationship in detail. It is the ability to form and maintain positive relationships with family, friends, teachers and others, and to end unhealthy relationships constructively. It involves trust, respect, cooperation, conflict resolution and understanding.

Empathy in detail. Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of another person, 'putting oneself in another's shoes'. It reduces prejudice and bullying, promotes kindness and helps in supporting people who are different or in difficulty.

Cooperation in detail. Cooperation means working together with others to achieve shared goals, sharing responsibilities, respecting others' contributions and resolving differences. Group projects, team games, cooperative learning and community service build this skill.

sections.title: Unit IV – Personal and Emotional Skills

blocks.text: Self-Awareness. Understanding one's strengths, weaknesses, feelings, values and behaviour.
Coping with Emotions. Recognising and managing emotions in healthy and constructive ways.
Coping with Stress. Using healthy strategies to manage pressure and demands.
Application. Life skills help learners handle study, relationships, personal choices and everyday challenges more effectively.

Self-awareness in detail. It is recognising one's own character, strengths, weaknesses, desires, values and emotions. It is the foundation of other life skills because it helps in setting goals, making decisions and understanding how one is influenced by others. Activities include self-reflection, journals, SWOT analysis and feedback.

Coping with emotions in detail. It involves recognising emotions in oneself and others, understanding their effects on behaviour and responding appropriately. Strategies include expressing feelings in healthy ways, anger management (counting, deep breathing, time-out), talking to trusted people and engaging in creative activities.

Coping with stress in detail. Stress arises from examinations, family problems, competition and relationships. Healthy strategies include time management, regular exercise, yoga and meditation, adequate sleep, balanced diet, hobbies, positive thinking, seeking social support and counselling. Unhealthy strategies like substance use must be avoided.

Application in detail. Life skills are applied in studies (planning, concentration), health (avoiding drugs, healthy habits), relationships (communication, empathy), career choice (decision-making), digital life (critical use of social media) and citizenship (cooperation, responsibility).

sections.title: LONG NOTES
Unit I – Life Skills

blocks.text: Life Skills: Abilities that help individuals deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life. Need and Importance: Life skills support healthy decisions, relationships, adjustment, confidence and responsible behaviour. Life Skills Education: An educational process for developing practical psychosocial abilities through participation and experience. Role of Education: Schools and teachers can deliberately develop life skills through activities, discussion, practice and reflection.

Meaning of life skills: Life skills, according to WHO, are abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that help individuals deal effectively with everyday challenges. The ten core life skills include self-awareness, empathy, critical and creative thinking, decision making, problem solving, communication, interpersonal relationships and coping with stress and emotions.

Need and importance: Adolescents face peer pressure, academic stress, substance abuse, relationship and career issues and online risks. Life skills help them make healthy choices, prevent risky behaviour, improve mental health and become confident, responsible citizens.

Life skills education: It uses participatory and experiential methods - role plays, discussions, case studies, games and projects - rather than lectures. It is part of programmes like the Adolescence Education Programme and the School Health Programme.

Role of education: Schools and teachers should create a supportive environment, integrate life skills into the curriculum and co-curricular activities, train teachers as facilitators, involve parents and provide counselling. NEP 2020 emphasises holistic development including these skills.

sections.title: Unit II – Thinking and Decision Skills

blocks.text: Critical Thinking: The ability to examine information and ideas carefully before accepting conclusions. Creative Thinking: The ability to generate new, useful and flexible ideas. Decision Making: The ability to choose among alternatives after considering possible consequences. Problem Solving: The ability to identify a problem, examine causes and alternatives and select a workable solution.
Critical thinking: Analysing information, questioning assumptions and evaluating evidence helps learners avoid misinformation and make informed choices.
Creative thinking: Generating original and flexible ideas helps learners adapt to change, solve problems in new ways and express themselves.
Decision making: A systematic process of identifying choices, considering consequences and choosing the best option helps in important life decisions about studies, health and relationships.

Problem solving: Defining a problem, exploring causes and alternatives, selecting and implementing a solution and reviewing results helps individuals handle challenges constructively. These thinking skills are interrelated and can be developed through open-ended questions, debates, projects and real-life case studies.

sections.title: Unit III – Social and Communication Skills

blocks.text: Effective Communication: Clear and appropriate expression together with careful listening and understanding. Interpersonal Relationship: The ability to establish and maintain healthy relationships with others. Empathy: The ability to understand another person's feelings and point of view. Cooperation: Working constructively with others toward shared goals.
Effective communication: Clear verbal and non-verbal expression, active listening and assertiveness help individuals express their needs and resist negative pressure.
Interpersonal relationships: The ability to build and maintain healthy relationships based on trust, respect and cooperation supports emotional well-being.
Empathy: Understanding others' feelings and perspectives promotes kindness, reduces conflict and bullying and helps people support each other.

Cooperation: Working together toward shared goals, sharing tasks and respecting others' contributions are essential in school, family, work and community. Group work, team sports and community service are effective ways to develop these social skills.

sections.title: Unit IV – Personal and Emotional Skills

blocks.text: Self-Awareness: Understanding one's strengths, weaknesses, feelings, values and behaviour. Coping with Emotions: Recognising and managing emotions in healthy and constructive ways. Coping with Stress: Using healthy strategies to manage pressure and demands. Application: Life skills help learners handle study, relationships, personal choices and everyday challenges more effectively.
Self-awareness: Knowing one's strengths, weaknesses, values and feelings is the foundation for setting goals and making good decisions.
Coping with emotions: Recognising and managing emotions such as anger, fear and sadness in healthy ways helps maintain relationships and mental health.
Coping with stress: Time management, exercise, relaxation, hobbies, positive thinking and seeking support help manage stress from studies and life events.

Application: Personal and emotional skills help learners manage studies, relationships, health choices and everyday challenges more effectively. When combined with thinking and social skills, they help young people lead balanced, healthy and productive lives.
